summary: Mars Walk is an interactive 3D map that helps a human explorer plan a Marswalk from Curiosity’s Bradbury Landing site to Yellowknife Bay, where NASA found evidence of an ancient habitable lake. It combines terrain and imagery from NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (credited with ESA’s Mars Express data), Curiosity’s drive history, and archived weather and radiation measurements from its REMS and RAD instruments. Users can reshape the 933 m route and see distance, climb, slope, and walking time, with each number labeled as computed, NASA-sourced, or assumed. Official IAU place names are separated from informal mission nicknames, stop cards link to NASA sources, and a first-person walkthrough follows the route. Conditions data is clearly marked archived, not live.
details:
What it does and how it works
Mars Walk is a web-based 3D map of Gale Crater for planning a Marswalk from Curiosity’s Bradbury Landing site to Yellowknife Bay, where NASA found evidence of an ancient habitable lake. It layers Mars terrain and imagery with named places, Curiosity’s real drive history, a computed slope-hazard map, and archived Curiosity weather and radiation data. Users can drag the route’s waypoints and see distance, ascent and descent, steepest slope, and estimated walking time update. An elevation profile follows the route, stop cards explain what is at each place with links to NASA sources, and a first-person mode walks the route at eye level.

Benefits and intended impact
It gives a prospective explorer one place to see route details, terrain, and conditions, with the source of every number visible. As a prototype, it shows how orbiter and rover data from several missions can be combined to support real planning decisions and make that planning easy to understand for the public.

Tools and technology
JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with Vite and CesiumJS, deployed on Vercel from GitHub. Data comes from NASA’s Mars Global Surveyor (MOLA) and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (CTX and HiRISE), ESA’s Mars Express (HRSC) via Cesium Mars, Curiosity positions from the NASA PDS PLACES archive, REMS weather data from PDS Atmospheres, RAD radiation data from PDS Planetary Plasma Interactions, and the USGS/IAU Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature. Developed on a MacBook Air (M3).

What makes it creative
Every number is tagged as computed from terrain, from a NASA source, or an assumption. Official IAU place names are visually separate from informal mission-team nicknames. The walking-pace model is editable. Yellowknife Bay was chosen because the destination itself has a real scientific story.

Factors considered

  • Honesty: conditions data is archived (the latest sol available is 4843, March 21, 2026) and is labeled as such, wind speed is shown as unavailable because the file flags it, and the 1 m terrain looks smooth up close because that is the data’s real limit.
  • Accuracy: slope values on a nearly flat plain are close to measurement noise, so they are described as estimates.
  • Accessibility: a text route summary, keyboard-accessible controls, and a checked color-contrast palette.
  • Performance: a Lite mode for lower-memory machines.
